profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab two days before a submission freeze for a workshop paper on large-learning-rate training. The team has a reproducibility problem: runs of a ResNet-32 on CIFAR-100 that are supposed to show the paper's key 'landscape flattening' effect instead show intermittent loss spikes after epoch 35 and inconsistent top-Hessian-eigenvalue traces across reruns. The meeting is between the lead PhD researcher who developed the analysis pipeline and the research engineer who maintained the training stack after a recent cluster image update. Their agenda is to diagnose why the instability plots no longer match prior figures, decide what the most plausible root cause is, and agree on a fix to rerun the core experiment that day. The expected outcome is an agreed troubleshooting plan, including what to rerun, what code path to patch, and what evidence will count as showing the issue is fixed.

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.expertise: optimization dynamics, loss landscape analysis, Hessian-spectrum estimation
members.background: Lina is the primary author of the workshop paper and built the original experimental pipeline for tracking sharpness during large-learning-rate SGD runs on vision models; she works mainly from analysis notebooks and lightly maintained training scripts derived from an older lab template.
members.private_state: She needs to recover plots consistent with the draft quickly and wants the issue to be framed as an implementation drift rather than a challenge to the paper's interpretation; she is especially worried that the observed loss spikes may undermine the narrative about flattening preceding instability.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing the 'instability run,' she means the canonical seed-7 CIFAR-100 run used in the draft figures, because that is the mentally privileged reference for all comparisons.
When she says 'sharpness,' she takes for granted that everyone means the top Hessian eigenvalue estimated on a fixed 2,048-example evaluation subset in eval mode.
A 'rerun of the baseline' naturally includes the old lab training container behavior, including the previous cuDNN convolution settings and data-loader seed handling.
If the loss curve is smooth again and the Hessian trace qualitatively matches the archived plot, that is enough to count as the issue being fixed for today's purposes.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: distributed training infrastructure, PyTorch performance tuning, experiment reproducibility
members.background: Arjun recently migrated the lab's training jobs to a new cluster image, cleaned up the launcher scripts, and added mixed-precision and throughput optimizations that were intended to preserve experiment semantics while making reruns faster and cheaper.
members.private_state: He wants to identify a concrete systems-level source of the mismatch without rolling back the whole stack, and he is concerned that the analysis code may be conflating training noise with actual curvature changes; he also wants any fix to be reproducible across seeds rather than tied to a single showcase run.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to the 'instability run,' they usually mean the current standard 5-seed sweep summary, not any one historically favored seed.

When someone says 'sharpness,' the operationally relevant quantity is whatever the monitoring job logs online during training, which in the current stack is a noisy power-iteration estimate computed on the latest training minibatch.
A 'baseline rerun' should use the current supported launcher and container unless someone explicitly requests a historical environment recreation.
A fix only counts if the instability symptoms disappear across at least the standard small seed sweep, because single-seed recoveries are too fragile to trust.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the instability run' and 'that run' as if discussing the same experiment instance.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring specifically to the archived seed-7 single run from March 18 that generated the draft figure with flattening before the spike.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the current default instability evidence: the aggregated behavior seen in the most recent 5-seed sweep launched after the cluster update.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have been immersed in the same project and there really is a salient instability phenomenon under discussion, so saying 'the run' sounds perfectly natural; neither expects that the other has silently switched the reference object from one canonical seed to a sweep summary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they should 'check whether the sharpness blows up before the loss spike.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the top Hessian eigenvalue from her offline Lanczos-style estimator on a fixed evaluation subset with dropout and batchnorm frozen in eval mode.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the online sharpness monitor in the training loop: a one-step power-iteration proxy on the current minibatch under training-mode dynamics.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In optimization meetings, 'sharpness' is a standard shared term, and both measurements are genuinely intended to capture curvature, so the surface agreement feels technical and precise even though the operational definitions differ materially.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'rerun the baseline with the old settings.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes recreating the historical software and runtime behavior that existed when the paper figures were made, including the old container, non-AMP training path, and prior deterministic defaults.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means keeping the same model, dataset, optimizer, and nominal hyperparameters, but within the current maintained stack and container, since environment rollback is outside the implied scope unless separately requested.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research labs, 'baseline' often colloquially means 'same experiment as before,' and both members think the omitted details are obvious from context; the disagreement hides in what each person considers part of the experiment identity versus mere execution plumbing.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both use the phrase 'if that stabilizes it, we're good.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 would count the problem as fixed if a single rerun reproduces the expected qualitative ordering of flattening, shift, and then instability closely enough to restore the paper figure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 would count it as fixed only if the patched setup removes the anomalous spikes or makes them consistent across the usual 3-5 seeds, indicating a robust root-cause correction rather than a lucky rerun.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely aiming to 'stabilize' the experiment, but one is anchored on recovering a narrative figure under deadline while the other is anchored on reproducibility standards; because they do not explicitly negotiate acceptance criteria, the phrase sounds fully aligned.
